timestralR

Run Mistral AI’s Timestral forecasting models from R — no Python, no PyTorch, no external runtime. The package downloads the official safetensors checkpoints from Mistral AI’s Hugging Face repositories and runs the transformer forward pass in a native RcppEigen backend (a pure-R reference implementation is included as a fallback). The forecasting loop — causal per-patch normalisation, two-stream time/variate attention, block decoding with median feedback, mirrored averaging, quantile capping and clipping — is a direct port of the official timestral Python package.

Install 

remotes::install_github("sjvrensburg/timestralR")
# or from a clone:
# R CMD INSTALL timestralR   (or devtools::install())

Requires R (>= 4.1) with a C++17 compiler; the hard R dependencies are jsonlite, digest and Rcpp/RcppEigen, plus the base packages utils, tools and stats. zoo, xts, tsibble, ggplot2, fabletools, fable and distributional are optional and only needed for the matching interfaces. Model weights are downloaded once per user on first use (21 MB for 5M up to 837 MB for 209M, fp32) and cached. Weights are Mistral AI’s, under their Modified MIT licence; package code is Apache 2.0, ported from Mistral AI’s Apache-2.0 timestral package.

Use

The vignette walks through every feature with plots: vignette("timestralR").

library(timestralR)
m  <- timestral_load("28M")                  # or a local directory or Hub repo ID
fc <- timestral_forecast(m, AirPassengers, h = 24)
plot(fc)                                     # fan chart: history + median + bands
timestral_median(fc)                         # a ts, starting Jan 1961
timestral_quantile(fc, 0.9)                  # any of fc$levels
fc$quantiles                                 # array: variate x step x 21 levels
head(as_forecast_df(fc))                     # tidy long format (with time column)

Inputs can be numeric vectors, ts/mts, zoo/xts (the time index is kept), matrices or data frames with time in rows, or a list of series forecast as a batch. Columns of a series are forecast jointly; NA marks missing values, and observation_mask can mark more.

# multivariate: columns are forecast jointly
fc2 <- timestral_forecast(m, cbind(mdeaths, fdeaths), h = 12)

# a batch of independent series in one call
fcb <- timestral_forecast(m, list(a = mdeaths, b = fdeaths), h = 12)

# covariates, time in rows: past-only over the context, known-future over
# the context plus the horizon (T + h rows)
y <- as.numeric(AirPassengers)
x <- seq_len(length(y) + 12)
fc3 <- timestral_forecast(m, y, h = 12,
                          past_covariates = log(y),
                          known_covariates = cbind(trend = x),
                          categorical_known_covariates = (x - 1) %% 12)

tidyverts and ggplot2 

library(tsibble)
library(fable)

# tsibble input: keys become the batch, measured variables the jointly
# forecast variates; rows are taken in index order and implicit gaps are
# filled with NA
fc <- timestral_forecast(m, as_tsibble(AirPassengers), h = 24)
as_tsibble(fc)                 # quantile columns, yearmonth index
as_fable(fc)                   # 21-quantile distributions
ggplot2::autoplot(fc)          # ggplot2 fan chart

# as a fable model, alongside the usual ones
as_tsibble(AirPassengers) |>
  model(timestral = TIMESTRAL(value, model = m), ets = ETS(value)) |>
  forecast(h = 24)

Forecasts from ts input get the same index class as tsibble::as_tsibble() gives the ts, so they join with and score against the observed data. Fitted TIMESTRAL() models keep a handle to the checkpoint rather than the weights, so mables stay small when saved and work in parallel workers.

forecast package and predict() 

fo <- forecast::forecast(m, AirPassengers, h = 24)   # a "forecast" object
forecast::accuracy(fo, test)                         # test-set measures
timestral_as_forecast(fc, level = c(80, 98))         # convert an existing forecast
predict(m, AirPassengers, h = 24)                    # same as timestral_forecast()
timestral_supports_known_covariates(m)               # can it use known-future covariates?

Evaluating forecasts 

bt <- timestral_backtest(m, AirPassengers, h = 12,       # forecast from each origin,
                         origins = seq(72, 132, by = 12)) # score against what followed
aggregate(cbind(ae, pinball, crps, cover80) ~ step, data = bt, FUN = mean)
timestral_score(fc, actual)                          # score a single forecast

Intervals are read off the quantile knots without interpolation, so each level must pair two knots: the default is 80% and 98%, since the 21 knots have no 2.5%/97.5% quantiles for 95%.

Validation

Parity against the official PyTorch package (timestral 1.0.0, torch 2.14.1 CPU, fp32 weights), twelve cases (missing values, negative trend without mirroring, multivariate, numeric covariates, horizon 1100, context 5000 capped to 4096 with horizon 2100, batch of 3, observation mask, categorical past/known/multivariate, non-default forecaster knobs), where max_rel is max abs difference over all quantiles/steps/variates relative to the largest official forecast value. Synthetic config variants (biases, gate-less, no-asinh) also match to < 2.3e-7; see docs/developer-notes.md:

model worst max_rel (case)
5M 2.0e-6 (long horizon)
28M 2.9e-7 (spot check, univariate)
123M 9.6e-6 (long context cap)
209M 2.6e-6 (long context cap)

Native-backend timings are in docs/developer-notes.md (209M: batch of 10 in 2.3 s, long-context worst case in 5.0 s on the development machine).

Reproduce with inst/parity_official.R (developer machine only; end users never need Python). One case is also gated in CI: the 5M univariate_missing forecast is committed as a golden fixture (tests/fixtures/{input,golden}_5m_univariate.csv, generated once by inst/make_5m_fixture.R from the official package) and the weekly real-checkpoint run asserts the native forecast matches it to the parity gate above.

Not yet supported

Nothing in the Python package’s inference surface: batched series, observation masks, numeric and categorical covariates, and all forecaster/loader options are supported. (Training and GPU execution are Python-side concerns with no R analogue.)

Development

Help pages and NAMESPACE are generated with roxygen2 (Rscript -e 'roxygen2::roxygenise()'); the native backend in src/ is split into one header and one implementation file per unit. Developer notes, including the source layout, the frozen internal interface and benchmarks, are in docs/developer-notes.md.
